paper.title: Refined Lower Bounds for Adversarial Bandits

settings.definition_quote: In every round $t \in \set{1,\ldots,T}$ the learner chooses a probability distribution $p_t$ ... The adversary then chooses a loss vector $\ell_t \in [0,1]^K$ ... Finally the learner samples an action from $p_t$ denoted by $I_t$ and observes her own loss $\ell_{I_t,t}$.

unmapped: loss sequences restricted to small-loss ball: L*_T <= alpha T

unmapped: loss sequences restricted to small quadratic variation: Q_T <= alpha T K

parameters.restriction: exists i* with l_{i*,t} = min_i l_{i,t} for all t

unmapped: a single arm is optimal in every round
settings.definition_quote: there is a loss sequence $\ell_{1:T} \in [0,1]^{K T}$ such that there exists an arm $i^*$ that is optimal at every round~$t$ (i.e., $\ell_{i^*,t} = \min_i \ell_{i,t}$ for all~$t \geq 1$)

extra_assumptions: Regret exceeds the bound with probability at least delta/2 (not delta)
Hard sequence has an arm optimal in every round and effective range <= sqrt((K-1)log(1/(4 delta))/T)/(4 sqrt(log 2))

source.label: thm:high-prob
source.quote: Suppose $K \geq 2$ and $\delta \in (0,1/4)$ and $T \geq 32 (K-1) \log(2/\delta)$, then there exists a sequence of losses $\ell_{1:T} \in [0,1]^{KT}$ such that \Pr{R_T(\ell_{1:T}) \geq \frac{1}{27} \sqrt{(K-1)T \log(1/(4\delta))}} \geq \delta/2, where the probability is taken with respect to the randomness in the algorithm.

results.notes: Probability of exceeding the bound is at least delta/2.

bound.regime: K >= 2, delta in (0,1/4), sqrt((K-1)/T) log(1/(4 delta)) <= C_exp, T >= 32 log(2/delta)

symbols.C_exp: constant such that the strategy satisfies E[R_T] <= C_exp sqrt((K-1)T) for all loss sequences

extra_assumptions: Applies to strategies with worst-case expected regret at most C_exp sqrt((K-1)T)
Probability of exceeding is at least delta/2

source.label: thm:high-prob-uniform
source.quote: Suppose $K \geq 2$, $T \geq 1$, and there exists a strategy and constant $C > 0$ such that for any $\ell_{1:T} \in [0,1]^{KT}$ it holds that $\E[R_T(\ell_{1:T})] \leq C \sqrt{(K-1)T}$. Let $\delta \in (0,1/4)$ satisfy $\sqrt{(K-1)/T} \log(1/(4\delta)) \leq C$ and $T \geq 32 \log(2/\delta)$. Then there exists $\ell_{1:T} \in [0,1]^{KT}$ for which \Pr{R_T(\ell_{1:T}) \geq \frac{\sqrt{(K-1)T}\log(1/(4\delta))}{203 C}} \geq \delta / 2

results.notes: Algorithm class: minimax-optimal-in-expectation strategies. Paper's C renamed C_exp.

bound.regime: K >= 2, T >= max(K,118), alpha in [max(c log(32T), K/2)/T, 1/2], c = 64/9

symbols.alpha_ball: radius of small-loss ball: L*_T <= alpha_ball * T

source.label: thm:firstorder-lowerbound
source.quote: Let $K \geq 2$, $T \geq K \vee 118$, and $\alpha \in \left[(c \log(32 T) \vee (K/2))/T, 1/2\right]$, where $c=64/9$. Then for any randomised bandit algorithm $\sup_{\ell_{1:T} \in \cB_{\alpha,T}} \E[\Reg_T(\ell_{1:T})] \geq \sqrt{\alpha T K} / 27$

symbols.alpha_ball: radius of small-variation ball: Q_T <= alpha_ball * T * K

source.label: thm:variation-lowerbound
source.quote: Let $K \geq 2$, $T \geq (32 K) \vee 601$, and $\alpha \in [(2 c_1 \log(T) \vee 8K)/T, 1/4]$, where $c_1 = (4/9)^2 (3\sqrt{5}+1)^2 \leq 12$. Then for any randomised bandit algorithm, $\sup_{\ell_{1:T} \in \cV_{\alpha,T}} \E[\Reg_T(\ell_{1:T})] \geq \sqrt{\alpha T K} / 25$

symbols.rho: effective range bound of the losses in each round

source.label: thm:impossibility-result-1
source.quote: Let $K \geq 2$, $T \geq 32(K-1)\log(14)$ and $\rho \geq 0.22 \sqrt{(K-1)/T}$. Then for any randomised bandit algorithm, $\sup_{\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_T \in \cC_{\rho}} \E[\Reg_T(\ell_{1:T})] \geq \sqrt{T (K-1)} / 504$

results.notes: Impossibility of regret scaling with effective range in bandit setting.

source.label: thm:impossibility-result-2
source.quote: Let $K \geq 2$ and $T \geq 32(K-1)\log(14)$. Then, for any randomised bandit algorithm, there is a loss sequence $\ell_{1:T} \in [0,1]^{K T}$ such that there exists an arm $i^*$ that is optimal at every round~$t$ ..., but $\E[\Reg_T(\ell_{1:T})] \geq \sqrt{T (K-1)} / 504$

results.notes: Existence of an always-optimal arm does not help in worst case.
